title: Athletic Stance and Ready Position
objective: Develop a balanced athletic stance that allows players to accelerate, decelerate or change direction efficiently in response to a football movement cue.
groundSize: One 4 × 4-metre movement square for every four players.
equipment: Coloured markers or coach signal cards
coachingDifficulty: 1 – Simple organisation; minimal observation or intervention required.
setup:
Create several 4 × 4-metre squares.
Position one player in the centre of each square.
Other players wait outside the square and rotate after each work period.
Players begin without a football before progressing to holding a football.
The coach stands where all players can see or hear the movement cues.
howTheDrillWorks:
Each player adopts an athletic ready position with feet slightly wider than hip width, knees flexed and bodyweight balanced through the middle of both feet.
The coach checks posture before calling a direction: forward, backward, left or right.
Players take two quick adjustment steps in the nominated direction and immediately reset into the ready position.
The coach varies the timing and order of the cues.
After four to six cues, players relax and another player enters the square.
Once technique is stable, players repeat while carrying a football in two hands.
Complete three to five short rounds per player.
coachingPoints: Keep the head upright and eyes forward rather than looking at the ground.
Maintain soft knees and hips so movement can begin immediately.
Keep the chest over the knees without bending excessively at the waist.
Distribute bodyweight evenly rather than leaning heavily onto the heels.
Use short adjustment steps when resetting.
Keep the feet active and avoid locking the legs.
When holding a football, keep it secure but away from the chest enough to permit natural arm movement.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether players can move in every direction without first shifting their bodyweight excessively.
Whether the knees remain aligned over the feet.
Whether the head and chest remain controlled during movement.
Whether players return to a balanced position after each cue.
Whether football security affects posture or movement quality.
progressions: Introduce visual colour cues instead of spoken directions.
Require a three-step acceleration before resetting.
Add a football and include a handball or kick after the final cue.
Pair players so one leads and the other mirrors.
Reduce the time between cues.
regressions: Use only forward and backward movement.
Allow players to walk through each direction before increasing speed.
Mark exact foot positions with flat markers.
Provide a demonstration before every repetition.
successIndicators: Begin in a balanced, repeatable athletic stance.
Move in any direction without a large preparatory step.
Keep their eyes forward while responding.
Reset under control after each movement.
Maintain football security without becoming rigid.
matchApplication: Australian football players frequently need to react from a stationary or low-speed position before leading, defending, collecting a loose football or responding to a turnover. A balanced ready position reduces reaction time and allows the player to move effectively in any direction.

title: Single-Leg Balance and Body Control
objective: Develop the single-leg balance and body control required to plant, pivot, sidestep, kick and recover after contact or an uneven possession.
groundSize: One 3 × 3-metre area for every pair.
coachingDifficulty: 2 – Basic coaching knowledge and one main teaching point.
setup:
Place players in pairs approximately three metres apart.
One player works while the partner observes and delivers the football.
Mark a central landing point for the working player.
Ensure adequate space between pairs.
Begin on a firm, level surface.
howTheDrillWorks:
The working player balances on one leg with the knee slightly flexed and eyes forward.
The partner gently handballs the football towards the player’s chest.
The player receives the football while maintaining single-leg balance for two seconds.
The player handballs back and resets.
Complete four receptions on each leg.
Progress to a small forward hop onto one leg before receiving.
Rotate roles after each set.
Complete two to four sets depending on the players’ age and ability.
coachingPoints: Land with the hip, knee and ankle aligned.
Keep the standing knee soft rather than locked.
Stabilise the hips so the opposite side does not drop excessively.
Keep the head and chest controlled.
Use the arms and football position to assist balance.
Absorb the landing quietly.
Regain balance before returning the football.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether the knee collapses inward during landing or balance.
Whether the player can stabilise before disposing of the football.
Whether one side is noticeably less controlled.
Whether players use unnecessary hopping to regain balance.
Whether receiving the football disrupts posture.
progressions: Increase the speed or variability of the handball.
Add a quarter-turn before landing.
Require the player to handball to a second moving target.
Add a controlled shoulder bump from a bump pad after the catch.
Use an uneven but safe surface such as a balance pad.
regressions: Allow the non-standing foot to touch the ground lightly.
Remove the hop and begin in a stationary position.
Use underarm football feeds rather than handballs.
successIndicators: Stabilise on either leg without repeated corrective hops.
Receive and release the football without losing posture.
Demonstrate improved balance on their weaker side.
matchApplication: Players regularly operate from one leg while kicking, stepping around opponents, reaching for loose footballs and recovering from physical pressure. Better single-leg control improves movement efficiency and reduces the likelihood of losing balance during critical skill actions.

title: Quick Feet Movement Grid
objective: Develop quick, controlled foot movements while maintaining an athletic posture and remaining prepared for the next football action.
groundSize: Multiple 5 × 5-metre grids.
coachingDifficulty: 2 – Basic coaching knowledge and one main teaching point.
setup:
Use flat markers to create a nine-square grid with three rows and three columns.
Each square should be approximately one metre wide.
Form a line of two to four players behind each grid.
Position a coach or feeder five metres beyond the grid.
Place footballs with the feeder.
howTheDrillWorks:
The first player enters the grid in an athletic stance.
The player follows a prescribed pattern through the squares, such as two feet in each square, lateral movement or forward-backward steps.
The player keeps the feet close to the ground and the body under control.
After exiting the grid, the player accelerates towards the feeder.
The feeder delivers a handball.
The player receives and returns the handball before jogging around the outside to rejoin the line.
Change the movement pattern every two rounds.
Continue until players have completed four to six patterns.
coachingPoints: Prioritise clean foot placement before maximum speed.
Keep the hips low enough to permit quick directional adjustment.
Avoid excessive upper-body movement.
Keep the head up whenever the pattern is understood.
Use the arms naturally for balance and rhythm.
Accelerate out of the grid rather than standing upright at the final marker.
Prepare the hands early for the football.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether foot placement remains accurate as speed increases.
Whether players maintain posture instead of looking continuously at the markers.
Whether players cross or tangle their feet during lateral patterns.
Whether the final acceleration is immediate.
Whether players can transition from footwork into a clean football skill.
progressions: Allow the coach to call the movement pattern as the player enters.
Add a visual cue indicating which side to exit.
Carry a football through the grid.
Add a passive defender after the grid.
Race two players through separate grids while retaining technical standards.
regressions: Practise one movement pattern at a time.
Permit players to watch their feet until the sequence is learned.
successIndicators: Complete each pattern without contacting markers.
Maintain balance and posture at increasing speed.
Keep their vision forward for most of the sequence.
matchApplication: Quick adjustment steps allow players to remain balanced in congestion, reposition around a stoppage, react to a bouncing football and prepare their body before receiving possession or applying pressure.

title: Controlled Deceleration and Stop
objective: Teach players to reduce speed safely and efficiently while remaining balanced and prepared to dispose of the football or change direction.
groundSize: Lanes measuring approximately 15 metres long and four metres wide.
coachingDifficulty: 2 – Basic coaching knowledge and one main teaching point.
setup:
Create several straight running lanes.
Mark a start line, acceleration zone and three-metre braking zone.
Place a feeder five metres beyond the braking zone.
Players form short lines at the start of each lane.
Ensure the braking surface is dry, level and free from hazards.
howTheDrillWorks:
The first player accelerates from the start line towards the braking zone.
On entering the braking zone, the player lowers the hips and uses several shorter steps to reduce speed.
The player stops under control before the final marker.
The feeder delivers a handball immediately after the stop.
The player receives and returns the football while maintaining balance.
The player exits the lane and rejoins the line.
Increase approach speed gradually across the rounds.
Complete four to six repetitions per player.
coachingPoints: Begin braking before reaching the final stopping point.
Reduce stride length progressively rather than taking one large stopping step.
Lower the hips and keep the chest controlled.
Keep the feet underneath the body.
Avoid allowing the knees to collapse inward.
Stay balanced after stopping.
Prepare the hands for the football before the body becomes completely stationary.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether players begin decelerating early enough.
Whether players use multiple braking steps.
Whether the final body position is balanced.
Whether knees and feet remain aligned.
Whether the player can execute a skill immediately after stopping.
progressions: Add a left or right exit after the stop.
Deliver the football before the player has fully stopped.
Require a kick after deceleration.
Use a visual stopping cue rather than a fixed braking zone.
Add a trailing defender providing controlled pressure.
regressions: Mark each braking step with flat markers.
Walk through the technique before running.
successIndicators: Reduce speed using several controlled steps.
Maintain hip, knee and ankle alignment.
Execute the following football skill cleanly.
matchApplication: Players must decelerate when approaching a loose football, preparing to kick, avoiding an opponent, leading towards the football or stopping before crossing the mark. Efficient braking permits faster play without sacrificing control.

title: First-Step Acceleration
objective: Develop an explosive and technically efficient first movement that allows players to create separation or reach the football before an opponent.
groundSize: Acceleration lanes measuring 10–15 metres long and four metres wide.
coachingDifficulty: 2 – Basic coaching knowledge and one main teaching point.
setup:
Mark several acceleration lanes.
Place one player at the beginning of each lane.
Position a feeder eight to ten metres ahead.
Place two coloured cones one metre to either side of the starting player.
Players waiting to rotate remain clear of the lanes.
howTheDrillWorks:
The player begins in the athletic ready position.
The coach calls or displays a colour corresponding to the left or right starting cone.
The player makes one quick adjustment step towards that cone.
The player immediately drives forward into a five-to-eight-metre acceleration.
The feeder handballs into the player’s path.
The player receives at speed and handballs back before slowing down.
Players rotate after every repetition.
Complete three to five starts from each side.
coachingPoints: Push forcefully into the ground with the first two steps.
Use a slight forward body angle without bending at the waist.
Keep the first steps short and powerful.
Drive the arms rather than allowing them to swing across the body.
Avoid standing upright too early.
React from a balanced stance.
Track the football without losing acceleration posture.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether the first movement is immediate.
Whether players push rather than reach with the lead foot.
Whether the body angle supports forward acceleration.
Whether arm action contributes to movement.
Whether players maintain speed while receiving the football.
progressions: Use random visual cues.
Begin from varied positions, including kneeling or side-on.
Add a competing player in a parallel lane.
Require a bounce or disposal after receiving.
Add a defender beginning one metre behind.
regressions: Practise the first three steps at controlled speed.
successIndicators: Maintain an effective forward body angle.
Receive the football without reducing speed significantly.
matchApplication: A strong first step helps players break from stoppages, lead towards the football, close defensive space, react to turnovers and create separation from direct opponents.

title: Plant-and-Cut Change of Direction
objective: Teach players to decelerate, plant safely and accelerate into a new direction without losing balance or exposing the body to unnecessary joint stress.
groundSize: Y-shaped lanes approximately 12 metres long and eight metres wide.
coachingDifficulty: 3 – Intermediate organisation, rotations and several observable behaviours.
setup:
Create a central running lane leading to a turning marker.
Place two exit gates five metres beyond the marker, one left and one right.
Position a coach behind the exit gates with two coloured markers.
Position a football feeder beyond each exit.
Players form a line at the start.
howTheDrillWorks:
The first player accelerates towards the central marker.
As the player approaches, the coach displays the colour corresponding to the left or right exit.
The player decelerates using short steps.
The player plants the outside foot beside the turning marker.
The hips and shoulders redirect towards the selected gate.
The player pushes away from the plant foot and accelerates through the gate.
A feeder delivers a handball after the change of direction.
The player returns the football and rotates out.
Complete three to five turns in each direction.
coachingPoints: Decelerate before attempting to redirect.
Place the plant foot outside the centre of mass without reaching excessively.
Keep the knee aligned over the foot.
Lower the hips during the plant.
Redirect the chest, hips and eyes towards the new direction.
Push forcefully away from the planted foot.
Accelerate for at least three steps after the turn.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether players arrive at the plant under control.
Whether the plant foot is positioned safely.
Whether the knee collapses inward.
Whether the hips and shoulders turn together.
Whether players accelerate immediately after changing direction.
progressions: Carry a football through the entire drill.
Add a passive defender at the turning point.
Allow three possible exit directions.
Require a bounce after the turn.
Use a chasing defender to create realistic pressure.
regressions: Practise the plant from a stationary position.
successIndicators: Maintain leg alignment during the cut.
Turn their body towards the new direction.
matchApplication: Change-of-direction skill is required when players separate from opponents, redirect leads, avoid congestion, defend a moving opponent or react to an unpredictable bounce or turnover.

title: Basic Sidestep Technique
objective: Teach players to use body movement, foot placement and acceleration to move an opponent away from the intended running line before escaping into available space.
groundSize: Lanes measuring approximately 12 × 5 metres.
coachingDifficulty: 3 – Intermediate organisation, rotations and several observable behaviours.
setup:
Create several narrow movement lanes.
Place a passive defender or upright pole in the centre of each lane.
Mark an exit gate on either side of the defender.
Position a football feeder at the beginning of the lane.
Attackers begin five metres from the defender.
howTheDrillWorks:
The feeder gives the attacker a short handball.
The attacker runs towards the passive defender with the football held securely in two hands.
Approximately two metres from the defender, the attacker lowers the hips and shows movement towards one side.
The attacker plants, shifts the body and exits through the opposite gate.
The attacker accelerates for three to five steps after the sidestep.
The defender initially remains stationary or provides only a hand target.
Players swap attacking and defending roles after each repetition.
Progressively allow the defender to shuffle and react within a restricted area.
coachingPoints: Approach with enough control to make a late decision.
Use the eyes, shoulders and hips to sell the false direction.
Keep the football secure and protected from the defender.
Plant close enough to redirect without overreaching.
Keep the knee aligned over the foot.
Move past the defender’s shoulder rather than directly sideways.
Accelerate immediately after the sidestep.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether the attacker approaches under control.
Whether the deception causes the defender to shift.
Whether the plant position is balanced and safe.
Whether the football remains protected.
Whether the attacker accelerates beyond the defender.
progressions: Allow the defender to react freely inside a two-metre zone.
Add a second defender after the first escape.
Require a handball or kick after the sidestep.
Use a chasing defender from behind.
Add a scoring gate that rewards forward movement.
regressions: Use a pole instead of a defender.
Practise the body fake without a football.
successIndicators: Cause the defender to shift or hesitate.
Protect the football through the movement.
matchApplication: Sidestepping allows a ball carrier to avoid a tackler, escape congestion, create time for disposal and maintain forward momentum when a direct running lane is blocked.

title: Scan-and-Move Reaction Grid
objective: Develop the ability to scan, identify an available movement option and respond quickly while maintaining control of the body and football.
groundSize: One 8 × 8-metre grid for every four to six players.
coachingDifficulty: 3 – Intermediate organisation, rotations and several observable behaviours.
setup:
Create an 8 × 8-metre square.
Mark a different coloured gate on each of the four sides.
Position one working player in the centre with a football.
Place a coach or signal player outside the grid.
Other players wait clear of the gates.
howTheDrillWorks:
The player begins in the centre in an athletic stance with the football in two hands.
The coach briefly displays a colour corresponding to one of the four gates.
The player scans, identifies the gate and moves towards it.
Before the player reaches the gate, the coach may display a second colour.
The player must decelerate, redirect and exit through the new gate.
After crossing the gate, the player handballs to a target positioned outside the grid.
The target returns the football to the next player.
Players rotate after each repetition.
Complete four to six repetitions each.
coachingPoints: Scan before beginning movement.
Keep the head stable enough to process the cue.
Move from a balanced stance.
Use controlled braking before redirecting.
Keep the football in two hands while options are changing.
Commit quickly once the final cue is recognised.
Accelerate through the selected gate.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether players genuinely scan rather than guess.
Whether the initial stance permits movement towards any gate.
Whether players remain balanced when the cue changes.
Whether the football is protected during redirection.
Whether players accelerate once the final option is known.
progressions: Add a defender who blocks one gate.
Use numbered or directional tactical cues instead of colours.
Require a kick to a moving target after exiting.
Introduce two players moving simultaneously.
Award points for correct and fast decisions.
regressions: Allow the player to walk before progressing to running speed.
successIndicators: Accelerate decisively through the available gate.
matchApplication: Players must constantly scan for opponents, teammates and space while moving. The ability to change a planned running line after receiving new information is essential when congestion shifts, a teammate becomes available or a defender closes an intended lane.

title: Ball-Carrying Movement Fundamentals
objective: Develop the ability to run, adjust direction and prepare for disposal while maintaining secure control of the football.
groundSize: Movement lanes approximately 20 metres long and five metres wide.
coachingDifficulty: 2 – Basic coaching knowledge and one main teaching point.
setup:
Create several lanes containing a start gate, two offset movement gates and a finishing gate.
Position the gates so players must make gradual directional adjustments.
Each player begins with a football.
Mark a bounce zone in the middle of the lane.
Position a target player five metres beyond the finishing gate.
howTheDrillWorks:
The first player runs through the start gate carrying the football securely in two hands.
The player moves through the first offset gate and transfers the football to the hand furthest from the imaginary pressure side.
The player completes a legal bounce inside the marked bounce zone.
The player changes direction through the second gate.
The player brings the football back to two hands before approaching the target.
The player handballs to the target and continues running to receive a return handball.
The next player begins when the lane is clear.
Rotate the target player after each group completes two repetitions.
coachingPoints: Carry the football in two hands when scanning or preparing to change direction.
Transfer the football away from the pressure side.
Keep the football close enough to protect but not pinned against the body.
Maintain natural running mechanics.
Bounce the football far enough ahead to continue moving.
Lift the eyes between each movement gate.
Prepare the hands and body early for disposal.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether the football remains secure during changes of direction.
Whether hand transfers are controlled.
Whether players look ahead rather than continuously at the football.
Whether the bounce supports continued movement.
Whether players keep running after disposing.
progressions: Add a passive defender beside one movement gate.
Allow the coach to nominate which gate must be used.
Require a kick at the finishing gate.
Add a second bounce.
Place a chasing defender behind the runner.
regressions: Replace the moving handball with a stationary target.
successIndicators: Maintain secure control of the football.
matchApplication: Ball carriers must protect possession while running through traffic, changing lanes, bouncing and preparing to handball or kick. Secure carrying technique allows players to move at speed without sacrificing awareness or disposal quality.

title: Defender Cue Evasion Decision
objective: Teach ball carriers to recognise a defender’s position and select an appropriate escape movement rather than using a predetermined evasion action.
groundSize: Movement channels measuring approximately 15 × 8 metres.
coachingDifficulty: 3 – Intermediate organisation, rotations and several observable behaviours.
setup:
Create a rectangular channel with one starting gate and two scoring gates at the opposite end.
Position one attacker at the starting gate with a football.
Place one defender five metres inside the channel.
The defender begins facing the attacker.
Place a support player beyond the scoring gates.
Form separate attacker and defender lines.
howTheDrillWorks:
The attacker enters the channel carrying the football in two hands.
The defender advances under controlled pressure and attempts to close one side of the channel.
The attacker scans the defender’s hips, movement line and available space.
The attacker chooses an appropriate response, which may include accelerating into space, changing direction or using a sidestep.
The attacker attempts to exit through either scoring gate without being touched with two hands by the defender.
After exiting, the attacker handballs to the support player.
The defender is initially restricted to shadowing and two-hand touch.
Players rotate from attacker to support, support to defender and defender to the waiting line.
Play six to ten repetitions before changing the defender’s starting position or rules.
coachingPoints: Approach with enough speed to threaten the defender but enough control to react.
Scan the defender’s hips rather than watching only the hands.
Attack the space the defender has surrendered.
Use a sidestep only when the defender commits.
Keep the football in two hands until the escape line is clear.
Protect the football on the side away from the defender.
Accelerate immediately after creating separation.
Avoid unnecessary movement when a direct running lane is available.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether the attacker scans before choosing a movement.
Whether the chosen action matches the defender’s position.
Whether the attacker carries the football securely.
Whether deception causes the defender to shift.
Whether the attacker accelerates after escaping.
Whether the defender applies safe and realistic pressure.
progressions: Allow the defender to apply full legal tackling appropriate to the group.
Add a second recovering defender.
Require the attacker to dispose to a moving target after escaping.
Reduce the width of the channel.
Award bonus points for escaping without losing forward momentum.
Add a support option so the attacker chooses between evasion and release.
regressions: Restrict the defender to lateral movement.
Predetermine which gate the defender must protect.
Replace the defender with a coach holding a bump pad.
Allow the attacker to begin closer to the scoring gates.
successIndicators: Scan the defender before selecting an action.
Choose the simplest effective escape option.
Create separation with one decisive movement.
matchApplication: A ball carrier rarely knows in advance whether the best option will be acceleration, a change of direction, a sidestep or an immediate disposal. This drill introduces the perception and movement connection required to evade pressure in open play, around stoppages and during transition.

title: Lateral Shuffle and Defensive Balance
objective: Develop efficient lateral movement that allows players to track an opponent or adjust position without crossing their feet or losing balance.
groundSize: Movement lanes approximately 8 metres wide and 4 metres deep.
coachingDifficulty: 2 – Basic coaching knowledge and one main teaching point.
setup:
Create several horizontal lanes with a central starting marker and a gate at each end.
Position one working player at the centre of each lane.
Place a coach or partner directly in front of the player.
Keep waiting players behind the lane.
Begin without footballs.
howTheDrillWorks:
The player begins in an athletic stance facing the coach.
The coach points left or right.
The player pushes from the opposite foot and shuffles towards the nominated gate.
The player keeps the hips and shoulders facing forward.
On the next signal, the player changes direction and shuffles towards the opposite gate.
After four to six signals, the player accelerates forward through the centre.
Players rotate after each work period.
Complete three to five rounds per player.
coachingPoints: Maintain a low, balanced stance.
Push from the inside edge of the foot opposite the movement direction.
Keep the feet apart rather than allowing them to come together.
Avoid crossing the feet during short lateral movements.
Keep the chest between the feet.
Maintain vision on the coach or opponent.
Use a controlled plant before reversing direction.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether the player moves by pushing rather than leaning.
Whether the feet cross during the shuffle.
Whether the hips remain low and stable.
Whether the player can reverse direction without standing upright.
Whether vision remains forward.
progressions: Use unpredictable visual signals.
Add a football handball immediately after the final shuffle.
Pair players for a mirror movement contest.
Add a forward or backward movement cue.
Introduce a controlled attacker for defensive tracking.
regressions: Practise one direction at a time.
Allow a reset at the centre after each movement.
successIndicators: Shuffle in either direction without crossing their feet.
Accelerate effectively after the lateral movement.
matchApplication: Lateral shuffle movement is used when corralling a ball carrier, protecting space around a stoppage, adjusting defensive position and delaying an opponent until support arrives.

title: Drop-Step Turn and Recovery
objective: Teach players to open their hips, turn efficiently and accelerate when an opponent or football moves behind their current body position.
groundSize: Lanes approximately 12 metres long and 5 metres wide.
coachingDifficulty: 3 – Intermediate organisation, rotations and several observable behaviours.
setup:
Mark a central starting point in each lane.
Place two turning gates behind the player, one to the left and one to the right.
Position a feeder beyond the turning gates.
The working player begins facing away from the feeder.
Other players form a short line outside the lane.
howTheDrillWorks:
The player begins in an athletic stance facing the coach.
The coach signals left or right.
The player drops the foot on the nominated side backwards.
The player opens the hips and turns through the selected side.
The player accelerates towards the corresponding rear gate.
The feeder handballs the football into the player’s path.
The player receives, returns the handball and exits the lane.
Players rotate after each repetition.
Complete three to five turns in each direction.
coachingPoints: Move the turning-side foot backwards rather than crossing it in front.
Open the hips before accelerating.
Keep the head controlled during the turn.
Maintain a low body position through the first movement.
Push forcefully from the ground after the turn.
Locate the football early.
Avoid spinning without gaining forward momentum.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether the first step creates space for the turn.
Whether the hips rotate cleanly.
Whether players remain balanced.
Whether the player finds the feeder early.
Whether acceleration begins immediately after turning.
progressions: Add a chasing player from the original starting position.
Use a moving feeder.
Require a kick after the turn.
Add a second directional cue during the recovery run.
Begin from a lateral shuffle before the drop step.
regressions: Practise the drop step from a stationary stance.
successIndicators: Open the hips with one efficient drop step.
Turn without crossing or tangling the feet.
Receive the football at running speed.
matchApplication: The drop step is important when a defender must turn and chase a leading forward, when the football travels over a player’s head or when a player must recover after being caught facing the wrong direction.

title: Crossover Step Acceleration
objective: Develop an efficient crossover step that allows players to accelerate rapidly from a square or lateral body position into open space.
groundSize: Lanes approximately 10 metres long and 6 metres wide.
coachingDifficulty: 2 – Basic coaching knowledge and one main teaching point.
setup:
Position the working player on a central marker facing the coach.
Place acceleration gates diagonally forward to the left and right.
Position a feeder beyond each gate.
Players wait behind the starting marker.
Use separate lanes where possible.
howTheDrillWorks:
The player begins square to the coach in an athletic stance.
The coach signals the left or right gate.
The player turns the hips towards the selected gate.
The opposite leg crosses in front to begin the acceleration.
The player drives through the gate using three to five powerful steps.
The feeder delivers a handball into the running line.
The player returns the football and rotates out.
Complete three to five repetitions in each direction.
coachingPoints: Turn the hips towards the intended line before crossing.
Keep the crossover step low and powerful.
Avoid twisting only through the shoulders.
Drive the outside arm to assist rotation.
Place the crossover foot towards the new running direction.
Accelerate through the gate rather than towards it.
Maintain balance during the transition.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether the hips turn before acceleration.
Whether the crossover step travels towards the gate.
Whether the player remains balanced.
Whether the first steps are powerful.
Whether the player receives without slowing.
progressions: Begin from a lateral shuffle.
Add a defender closing one gate.
Carry a football through the movement.
Use a second cue to change the finishing direction.
Race two players from parallel starting positions.
regressions: Practise the crossover at walking speed.
Mark the first two foot placements.
successIndicators: Rotate the hips towards the target.
matchApplication: A crossover step allows players to break quickly from a stoppage, react to a loose football, chase an opponent or accelerate from a defensive square position into a forward-running line.

title: Pivot and Reorient
objective: Develop the ability to pivot under control and reorient the body towards a new target while maintaining balance and possession.
groundSize: Circular or square areas approximately 6 × 6 metres.
coachingDifficulty: 3 – Intermediate organisation, rotations and several observable behaviours.
setup:
Position one player in the centre of a marked area with a football.
Place three target players around the outside.
Assign each target a different colour or number.
The working player begins facing one target.
Keep the central area clear.
howTheDrillWorks:
The central player holds the football in two hands.
The coach calls a colour or number.
The player scans to locate the nominated target.
The player plants one foot and pivots around it.
The hips and shoulders turn towards the target.
The player completes a handball to the target.
The target returns the football immediately.
The coach nominates another target.
Rotate the central player after six to eight disposals.
coachingPoints: Establish balance before pivoting.
Keep the pivot foot connected to the ground without locking the knee.
Turn through the hips rather than twisting only the upper body.
Keep the football close and protected during the turn.
Move the non-pivot foot in a controlled arc.
Finish square to the target.
Scan before beginning the disposal action.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether the player identifies the target before disposing.
Whether the pivot foot remains stable.
Whether balance is maintained.
Whether the hips and shoulders reorient together.
Whether the disposal begins only after the body is organised.
progressions: Add a passive defender applying arm pressure.
Require a kick after the pivot.
Use moving targets.
Add a fake towards one target before turning to another.
Limit the decision time.
regressions: Allow a complete reset between cues.
successIndicators: Protect the football during the turn.
matchApplication: Players pivot when trapped near the boundary, turning away from pressure, reorienting after a mark or changing the direction of ball movement when the original option closes.

title: Stop-Start Pace Change
objective: Teach players to use controlled changes of pace to unbalance an opponent and create separation without relying solely on a change of direction.
groundSize: Straight lanes approximately 18 metres long and 4 metres wide.
coachingDifficulty: 3 – Intermediate organisation, rotations and several observable behaviours.
setup:
Mark a start gate, control zone and finishing gate in each lane.
Position one attacker at the start with a football.
Place a passive defender one metre behind the attacker.
The defender initially follows without attempting to touch.
Players form separate attacker and defender lines.
howTheDrillWorks:
The attacker begins running at approximately 70 per cent speed.
On entering the control zone, the attacker reduces speed while remaining balanced.
The attacker waits for the defender to reduce speed.
The attacker then accelerates sharply towards the finishing gate.
The defender attempts to follow the pace change.
The attacker handballs to a target beyond the gate.
Players swap roles after each repetition.
Complete four to six repetitions each.
coachingPoints: Reduce pace without becoming stationary unless deliberately using a full stop.
Maintain an athletic posture while slowing.
Keep the football secure in two hands.
Observe the defender’s speed and body position.
Accelerate when the defender’s momentum has reduced.
Use powerful first steps during reacceleration.
Continue forward after creating separation.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether the attacker changes pace noticeably.
Whether balance is retained during the slowdown.
Whether the acceleration is timed to the defender’s reaction.
Whether the football remains protected.
Whether separation is created.
progressions: Allow the defender to apply two-hand touch pressure.
Permit the attacker to use multiple pace changes.
Add a decision between stop-start and sidestep.
Require a kick after the escape.
Add a second recovering defender.
successIndicators: Produce a clear and controlled pace change.
Recognise when the defender has slowed.
matchApplication: Changes of pace help forwards create separation on a lead, ball carriers escape trailing defenders and players move through congestion without always needing a major directional change.

title: Shoulder and Hip Feint
objective: Develop the use of the eyes, shoulders and hips to move a defender away from the intended escape line before accelerating into space.
groundSize: Channels approximately 12 × 6 metres.
coachingDifficulty: 3 – Intermediate organisation, rotations and several observable behaviours.
setup:
Mark one starting gate and two exit gates.
Position a defender between the attacker and the exit gates.
The attacker begins with a football.
The defender initially remains inside a one-metre movement zone.
Form separate attacker and defender lines.
howTheDrillWorks:
The attacker approaches the defender under control.
The attacker looks and moves the shoulders and hips towards one exit.
The defender reacts laterally within the restricted zone.
The attacker plants and accelerates through the opposite exit.
The attacker keeps the football protected away from the defender.
The defender attempts a two-hand touch after reacting.
Players rotate roles after each repetition.
Complete three to five attacks from each side.
coachingPoints: Approach close enough to influence the defender.
Use the eyes, shoulders and hips together.
Keep the feet underneath the body during the fake.
Avoid leaning so far that recovery becomes slow.
Watch the defender’s hips for a genuine reaction.
Move immediately once the defender commits.
Accelerate past the defender’s outside shoulder.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether the attacker’s body language is convincing.
Whether the defender reacts to the feint.
Whether the attacker remains balanced.
Whether the escape begins immediately.
Whether the football is protected.
progressions: Remove the defender’s movement restriction.
Allow either a body feint or pace change.
Add a second defender after the exit gate.
Require a disposal to a moving target.
Reduce the channel width.
regressions: Use an upright pole instead of a defender.
Predetermine the fake and escape sides.
Practise the shoulder and hip movement without a football.
successIndicators: Cause the defender to shift or hesitate.
matchApplication: Body feints are used to move tacklers, create disposal space and manipulate opponents without requiring a large sidestep that may slow forward momentum.

title: Hand Transfer and Ball Protection
objective: Teach players to transfer and position the football away from pressure while maintaining running speed and readiness to dispose.
groundSize: Lanes approximately 15 metres long and 5 metres wide.
coachingDifficulty: 3 – Intermediate organisation, rotations and several observable behaviours.
setup:
Create straight running lanes with a pressure zone in the middle.
Position an attacker at the start with a football.
Place a defender beside the pressure zone.
The defender is restricted to shadow pressure or presenting a hand target.
Place a receiver beyond the finishing gate.
howTheDrillWorks:
The attacker runs towards the pressure zone with the football in two hands.
The defender steps towards either side of the attacker.
The attacker identifies the pressure side.
The attacker transfers the football to the hand or side furthest from the defender.
The attacker turns the torso slightly to place the body between the defender and football.
The attacker accelerates through the finishing gate.
The attacker returns the football to two hands and handballs to the receiver.
Players rotate through attacker, defender and receiver roles.
coachingPoints: Begin with the football in two hands.
Scan the defender before transferring.
Move the football early enough to avoid reaching across pressure.
Keep the elbows and football close to the body.
Use the torso and shoulder as a legal protective barrier.
Maintain running rhythm.
Return to two hands before disposing.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether the attacker recognises the pressure side.
Whether the transfer is controlled.
Whether the player protects legally.
Whether running speed is maintained.
Whether the football returns to a disposal-ready position.
progressions: Allow controlled body contact.
Add a second defender on the opposite side.
Require a bounce after the transfer.
Add a sidestep before the handball.
Require the attacker to choose between protecting and releasing to support.
regressions: Use a bump pad instead of a player.
successIndicators: Position the body between opponent and football.
matchApplication: Players must protect the football when running past opponents, absorbing pressure after a ground-ball collection or attempting to break into space before disposing.

title: Mirror Reaction Footwork
objective: Develop rapid movement responses by requiring players to read and mirror an opponent’s unpredictable changes of direction and pace.
groundSize: One 6 × 4-metre rectangle per pair.
coachingDifficulty: 3 – Intermediate organisation, rotations and several observable behaviours.
setup:
Create multiple rectangular grids.
Position two players facing each other approximately two metres apart.
Nominate one player as the leader and one as the mirror.
The leader may move laterally, forwards or backwards within the grid.
Keep work periods short and intense.
howTheDrillWorks:
Both players begin in an athletic stance.
On the coach’s signal, the leader moves unpredictably within the grid.
The mirror attempts to maintain the same relative position.
The leader may change pace and direction but must remain under control.
After eight to twelve seconds, the coach calls “go”.
The leader attempts to escape through either side gate.
The mirror attempts to reach the same gate within one step.
Players rest briefly and swap roles.
Complete four to six rounds each.
coachingPoints: Watch the opponent’s hips and centre of mass.
Maintain a stance that allows movement in every direction.
Use short steps while tracking.
Avoid guessing before the leader commits.
Decelerate before reversing.
Accelerate decisively when the escape begins.
Maintain balance under repeated direction changes.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether the mirror maintains appropriate distance.
Whether players react to movement rather than anticipate blindly.
Whether footwork remains controlled.
Whether players can change direction repeatedly.
Whether the final acceleration is immediate.
progressions: Give the leader a football.
Allow the leader to use body feints.
Add a handball target after the escape.
Increase the grid size.
Award points for successful escapes or defensive matches.
regressions: Place a line between the players to maintain spacing.
successIndicators: Match repeated direction and pace changes.
Stay balanced without unnecessary crossing steps.
React quickly to the final escape.
Demonstrate controlled movement on both sides.
matchApplication: Reactive mirror movement develops the tracking skills required to defend a ball carrier, follow a leading opponent, apply pressure and respond to sudden movement changes around stoppages.

title: Gate Recognition and Escape
objective: Develop the ability to recognise an open running gate and select the fastest controlled movement to escape through it.
groundSize: One 10 × 10-metre grid for every five to six players.
coachingDifficulty: 4 – Advanced tactical coaching, live constraints and active correction.
setup:
Create a square grid with one gate on each side.
Position one attacker with a football in the centre.
Place two defenders inside the grid.
Defenders begin three metres from the attacker.
A coach stands outside and can close one gate by raising a coloured marker.
Position receivers outside the remaining gates.
howTheDrillWorks:
The attacker begins in the centre with the football in two hands.
On the coach’s signal, the defenders move to pressure the attacker.
The coach simultaneously closes one gate.
The attacker scans the defenders and the available gates.
The attacker chooses an escape line using acceleration, change of direction, pace change or body feint.
The attacker scores by exiting an open gate without being touched with two hands.
The attacker handballs to the receiver outside the gate.
Defenders score by touching the attacker before the exit.
Rotate the attacker and defenders every two repetitions.
coachingPoints: Scan before the defenders arrive.
Identify the largest available space rather than automatically selecting the nearest gate.
Keep the football in two hands while options remain open.
Use the simplest movement that solves the problem.
Avoid running directly towards both defenders.
Manipulate one defender to create a larger gap.
Accelerate fully once the gate is selected.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether the attacker scans all gates.
Whether the selected gate is genuinely available.
Whether the movement choice fits the defensive position.
Whether the attacker protects the football.
Whether the attacker commits decisively after choosing.
progressions: Allow controlled tackling.
Close two gates.
Add a support player inside the grid.
Require a kick after exiting.
Introduce a recovering defender outside the gate.
Add a time limit.
regressions: Permit defenders to walk or shadow only.
matchApplication: Players must identify and attack available space when escaping stoppages, carrying through congestion, reacting to a turnover or finding a path around several defenders.

title: Movement Fundamentals Circuit Assessment
objective: Assess each player’s ability to combine the fundamental movement skills developed through EA-001 to EA-019 in a controlled football-specific circuit.
groundSize: An area approximately 30 × 20 metres divided into five assessment stations.
coachingDifficulty: 4 – Advanced tactical coaching, live constraints and active correction.
setup:
Create five stations:
Ready Position and Reaction: Four-direction movement from a central marker.
Acceleration and Deceleration: Sprint into a controlled stopping zone.
Change of Direction: React to a left or right gate and execute a plant-and-cut.
Ball Protection and Evasion: Carry through controlled defender pressure.
Scan and Escape: Select an open gate against one or two defenders.
Divide players evenly between stations.
Assign a coach or observer to each station where possible.
Use a simple rating of Developing, Competent or Advanced for each skill area.
Complete one familiarisation repetition before scoring.
howTheDrillWorks:
Players begin at their assigned station.
Each player completes two assessed repetitions.
The coach records movement quality rather than relying only on completion time.
Players rotate clockwise after all group members finish.
At the reaction station, players respond to three random cues while maintaining posture.
At the acceleration station, players sprint ten metres and stop inside the marked zone.
At the change-of-direction station, players react to a visual gate cue and accelerate after planting.
At the protection station, players carry past controlled side pressure and dispose to a target.
At the escape station, players identify and attack an available gate.
Coaches provide brief feedback after the second repetition.
Complete all five stations before finishing with a short group review.
coachingPoints: Assess movement quality before maximum speed.
Look for balanced starting and finishing positions.
Observe both left- and right-side capability.
Check whether players scan before acting.
Monitor knee, hip and ankle alignment.
Assess football security under movement pressure.
Reward decisive acceleration after each movement.
Record recurring weaknesses for future individual coaching.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Athletic stance and movement readiness.
Balance during acceleration, stopping and turning.
Foot placement during lateral movement and change of direction.
Ability to use both sides of the body.
Scanning and reaction to visual information.
Selection of an appropriate evasion action.
Football security during movement.
Ability to accelerate after the final decision.
progressions: Compare results across multiple testing dates.
Add match-like legal contact for advanced groups.
Add disposal accuracy scoring.
Introduce fatigue before the second circuit.
Use timed results alongside technical ratings.
Add positional versions for defenders, midfielders and forwards.
regressions: Complete stations individually rather than as a continuous circuit.
Assess without a football before adding possession.
successIndicators: Begin from a balanced athletic stance.
Change direction safely from both sides.
Scan and select appropriate movement options.
Protect the football under controlled pressure.
Demonstrate no major technical breakdown across the circuit.
matchApplication: The circuit combines the core movement abilities required to react, accelerate, stop, redirect, protect possession and evade opponents. The results allow coaches to identify whether players are ready to progress into more dynamic movement, pressure and match-simulation drills.
relatedDrills: EA-001 – Athletic Stance and Ready Position

title: Curved Lead Acceleration
objective: Develop the ability to accelerate along a curved lead that creates separation while allowing the player to see both the football and the space ahead.
groundSize: Leading lanes approximately 20 metres long and 10 metres wide.
coachingDifficulty: 3 – Intermediate organisation, rotations and several observable behaviours.
setup:
Mark one starting position, a curved line of three guide cones and a receiving gate.
Position a kicker approximately 20 metres from the receiving gate.
Place the working player five metres inside the first guide cone.
Position a return player behind the kicker.
Create several identical lanes where numbers allow.
howTheDrillWorks:
The working player begins in an athletic stance and scans the space around the receiving gate.
On the kicker’s movement cue, the player accelerates towards the first guide cone.
The player follows a curved running line through the remaining cones.
The player keeps the chest partially open towards the kicker while continuing to accelerate.
The kicker delivers the football into the receiving gate.
The player marks at speed, turns towards the return player and completes a kick or handball.
The player follows the disposal and rotates to the return position.
The kicker becomes the next leading player.
Complete leads from both left and right sides.
coachingPoints: Begin the lead with a decisive first movement.
Use the curve to preserve vision of the football.
Accelerate through the entire lead rather than slowing before the mark.
Keep the body balanced while changing the running angle.
Show the kicker a clear target with the hands.
Time the lead to the kicker’s preparation.
Reorient quickly after marking.
Use both sides of the ground.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether the lead begins at the correct time.
Whether the player maintains vision of the kicker.
Whether the curved line creates useful separation.
Whether the player slows before receiving.
Whether the player can reorient and dispose quickly.
progressions: Add a trailing defender.
Remove the guide cones.
Allow the kicker to choose between two curved leads.
Require a kick to a second moving player after the mark.
Begin with a double movement before the curved lead.
regressions: Use a handball feed instead of a kick.
Keep the guide cones in place for all repetitions.
successIndicators: Time the lead to the ball carrier.
Accelerate along a controlled curved path.
matchApplication: Curved leads allow forwards and supporting players to create separation while remaining connected to the ball carrier. They are particularly useful when leading towards the boundary, changing the kicking angle or opening space for another player.

title: Double-Movement Lead
objective: Teach players to use an initial false lead and sharp second movement to create separation from a tracking defender.
groundSize: Leading channels approximately 20 × 10 metres.
coachingDifficulty: 3 – Intermediate organisation, rotations and several observable behaviours.
setup:
Mark a starting position for one attacker and one defender.
Place two possible receiving gates eight metres apart.
Position a kicker 20–25 metres from the gates.
The defender begins one metre behind or beside the attacker.
Create a safe deceleration area between the gates.
howTheDrillWorks:
The attacker begins with the defender in close tracking position.
On the kicker’s preparation, the attacker makes a strong initial lead towards one gate.
The defender shadows the first movement.
Before reaching the gate, the attacker decelerates, plants and changes direction.
The attacker accelerates towards the opposite gate.
The kicker delivers the football to the second lead.
The attacker attempts to mark before the defender can recover.
The attacker returns the football and swaps roles with the defender.
Rotate the kicker regularly.
coachingPoints: Make the first lead convincing enough to move the defender.
Change pace as well as direction.
Decelerate before planting.
Maintain safe hip, knee and ankle alignment.
Turn the head early to locate the kicker.
Accelerate immediately into the second lead.
Keep the second running line clear of the defender.
Deliver the kick only after separation is created.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether the first lead causes the defender to commit.
Whether the attacker decelerates under control.
Whether the direction change is decisive.
Whether the second acceleration creates separation.
Whether the kicker recognises the correct delivery time.
progressions: Allow the defender to apply full match-like tracking pressure.
Remove the receiving gates.
Allow the attacker to choose whether to continue the first lead or use the second.
Add a second attacker whose movement must remain coordinated.
Require immediate play-on after the mark.
regressions: Practise the movement without a football delivery.
successIndicators: Commit fully to the first lead.
Move the defender away from the intended space.
Accelerate sharply on the second movement.
matchApplication: Double movements are used by forwards, midfielders and defenders when an opponent is tracking closely. A convincing first movement can move the defender off balance and open a more dangerous receiving lane.

title: V-Cut Separation
objective: Develop a sharp V-cut lead that moves a defender towards one area before creating separation back towards the football carrier.
groundSize: Triangular areas approximately 15 metres long and 10 metres wide.
coachingDifficulty: 3 – Intermediate organisation, rotations and several observable behaviours.
setup:
Mark a starting point, an away marker and a receiving gate to form a V-shaped path.
Position the kicker 15–20 metres from the receiving gate.
Place one attacker and one defender at the starting point.
The defender begins in a controlled trailing position.
Create multiple stations where possible.
howTheDrillWorks:
The attacker accelerates away from the kicker towards the away marker.
The defender follows the attacker’s movement.
Near the marker, the attacker decelerates using short steps.
The attacker plants the outside foot and turns sharply back towards the kicker.
The kicker delivers the football into the receiving gate.
The attacker accelerates towards the football and attempts to mark in front.
The defender provides controlled pressure without holding.
Players rotate through attacker, defender and kicker roles.
Perform the V-cut from both sides.
coachingPoints: Run hard enough away from the kicker to move the defender.
Decelerate before the plant.
Keep the plant foot close enough to the body for balance.
Turn the hips, chest and eyes towards the football.
Drive out of the cut with short, powerful steps.
Protect the leading lane with legal body positioning.
Present the hands early.
Ensure the kick favours the attacker’s new running line.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether the away movement is convincing.
Whether the plant is controlled and safe.
Whether the player turns the whole body.
Whether the return acceleration is immediate.
Whether the attacker gains front position.
progressions: Allow the attacker to choose between continuing away or making the V-cut.
Add full defensive pressure appropriate to the group.
Remove the guide markers.
Require a kick after the mark.
Coordinate two simultaneous V-cut leads.
successIndicators: Move the defender away from the football.
Turn efficiently back towards the kicker.
matchApplication: V-cuts create separation when a player is closely guarded and needs to lead back towards the football. They are common during forward entries, kick-ins and possession movement along the boundary.

title: Lateral Receive and Reorient
objective: Develop the ability to receive a football while moving laterally and immediately reorient towards the next attacking direction.
groundSize: Rectangular grids approximately 12 × 8 metres.
coachingDifficulty: 3 – Intermediate organisation, rotations and several observable behaviours.
setup:
Position a feeder at one end of the grid.
Place a receiver on a central starting marker.
Mark one lateral receiving gate on each side.
Position a target player beyond the opposite end of the grid.
The feeder holds several footballs.
howTheDrillWorks:
The receiver begins facing the feeder.
The feeder signals the left or right receiving gate.
The receiver moves laterally towards the nominated gate.
The feeder handballs the football ahead of the receiver.
The receiver catches while moving and keeps the feet active.
The receiver pivots or turns towards the forward target.
The receiver accelerates for two or three steps and handballs to the target.
The receiver follows the disposal and becomes the target.
The target returns to the feeder line.
Repeat from both sides.
coachingPoints: Move before the football is released.
Present the hands early.
Cushion the football without stopping the feet.
Scan the forward target before receiving.
Keep the hips low during reorientation.
Turn towards the attacking direction rather than back towards pressure.
Accelerate after completing the turn.
Dispose while maintaining forward movement.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether the player creates movement before reception.
Whether the football is caught cleanly.
Whether the feet remain active.
Whether the player turns efficiently towards the target.
Whether the disposal occurs with forward momentum.
progressions: Add a passive defender behind the receiver.
Use a kick instead of a handball feed.
Allow the target to move into either of two gates.
Require the receiver to decide whether to turn inside or outside.
Add a second disposal after the first handball.
regressions: Allow the player to stop before turning.
successIndicators: Continue the ball movement at speed.
matchApplication: Players often receive while moving sideways around congestion, stoppages and defensive structures. Quickly turning towards the next attacking option prevents the movement from becoming slow or backward.

title: Give-and-Go Running Support
objective: Develop the habit of accelerating into a new support position immediately after disposing of the football.
groundSize: Channels approximately 20 metres long and 6 metres wide.
coachingDifficulty: 3 – Intermediate organisation, rotations and several observable behaviours.
setup:
Position Player A at the start with a football.
Position Player B approximately six metres ahead.
Position Player C another eight metres forward.
Mark a running lane past the outside shoulder of Player B.
Create several groups of three.
howTheDrillWorks:
Player A accelerates towards Player B.
Player A handballs to Player B and immediately runs past on the nominated side.
Player B receives, protects the football and waits until Player A reaches a forward support position.
Player B returns the handball into Player A’s running path.
Player A receives at speed and handballs to Player C.
Player A follows the disposal to Player C’s position.
Player B moves to the starting position.
Player C carries the football back or begins the drill in the opposite direction.
Alternate the side of the running support.
coachingPoints: Accelerate immediately after the first disposal.
Run past the receiver’s outside shoulder.
Communicate the intended running side.
Return the football into space rather than directly at the runner.
Keep the receiver moving forward.
Avoid running too close to the teammate.
Maintain legal running distance and bounce requirements in longer versions.
Continue moving after the second disposal.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether Player A accelerates after handballing.
Whether the support line is wide enough.
Whether communication occurs early.
Whether the return handball leads the runner.
Whether the sequence maintains forward momentum.
progressions: Add a chasing defender.
Remove the nominated running side.
Add a second give-and-go action.
Require a kick after the return handball.
Use two groups moving through adjoining lanes.
regressions: Use stationary return handballs before leading the runner.
successIndicators: Run into a clear support lane.
Deliver the return handball into space.
matchApplication: Give-and-go movement creates numerical overlap, allows players to escape pressure and keeps the original ball carrier involved after disposal. It is central to effective handball chains and transition football.

title: Outside Overlap Running Lane
objective: Teach players to create an outside overlap by timing their run to receive beyond a teammate and continue forward ball movement.
groundSize: Channels approximately 25 metres long and 12 metres wide.
coachingDifficulty: 3 – Intermediate organisation, rotations and several observable behaviours.
setup:
Mark an inside ball-carrying lane and a wider outside overlap lane.
Position Player A at the start with a football.
Position Player B five metres ahead in the inside lane.
Position Player C behind and outside Player A.
Place a finishing target near the end of the channel.
howTheDrillWorks:
Player A moves forward and handballs to Player B.
As the football travels, Player C accelerates through the outside lane.
Player B receives and continues moving forward.
Player C communicates and runs beyond Player B’s shoulder.
Player B handballs into Player C’s running path.
Player C receives outside the original ball line.
Player C carries forward and disposes to the finishing target.
All players follow their disposal and rotate forward one position.
Repeat on the opposite side.
coachingPoints: Begin the overlap run late enough to arrive at speed.
Maintain genuine width from the inside ball carrier.
Run beyond the receiver before calling for the football.
Communicate clearly and early.
Deliver the handball in front of the overlapping player.
Keep the ball carrier moving to engage imaginary pressure.
Receive with vision towards the next target.
Continue forward after the overlap.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether the overlap begins at the correct time.
Whether the runner maintains sufficient width.
Whether Player B draws the football inside before releasing.
Whether the handball leads the runner.
Whether the final disposal retains forward momentum.
progressions: Add an inside defender who pressures Player B.
Allow the ball carrier to choose between the overlap and an inside target.
Remove the marked lanes.
Add a kick to a leading forward.
Create consecutive overlaps involving four players.
regressions: Begin the overlap runner level with Player A.
successIndicators: Time the overlap to arrive at speed.
Run beyond the current ball carrier.
matchApplication: Outside overlap running helps teams move around defensive pressure, use width and create an unpressured ball carrier during transition or possession chains.

title: Inside Underlap Support Run
objective: Develop an inside support run that allows a player to move underneath a wider ball carrier and receive through a central attacking lane.
groundSize: Channels approximately 25 metres long and 12 metres wide.
coachingDifficulty: 4 – Advanced tactical coaching, live constraints and active correction.
setup:
Mark a wide ball-carrying lane and a narrower inside lane.
Position Player A with the football in the wide lane.
Position Player B slightly behind and inside Player A.
Place Player C as a forward target at the end of the channel.
Mark an inside receiving gate approximately 12 metres ahead.
howTheDrillWorks:
Player A carries the football forward through the wide lane.
Player B initially runs outside Player A’s direct vision.
As Player A approaches the receiving gate, Player B accelerates diagonally underneath into the inside lane.
Player B communicates and presents in front of Player A.
Player A handballs into the inside running path.
Player B receives at speed and continues through the central gate.
Player B disposes to Player C.
Players rotate forward through the positions.
Repeat from the opposite side of the ground.
coachingPoints: Begin behind the ball carrier before accelerating inside.
Time the run so the inside lane is reached at speed.
Avoid crossing too close to the ball carrier.
Scan for defenders or teammates occupying the corridor.
Communicate before entering the ball carrier’s vision.
Lead the runner with the handball.
Continue forward rather than receiving flat.
Use the underlap only when the inside lane is genuinely available.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether the runner begins from behind the ball.
Whether the inside cut is timed correctly.
Whether safe spacing is maintained.
Whether the ball carrier scans before releasing.
Whether the receiver enters the corridor with forward momentum.
progressions: Add a defender protecting the inside lane.
Allow Player B to choose between overlap and underlap.
Remove the marked lanes.
Add a recovering defender from behind.
Require a kick inside 50 after receiving.
successIndicators: Begin from behind the ball carrier.
Receive in front and at speed.
Continue the football through the central corridor.
matchApplication: An underlap can exploit space inside a wide ball carrier, connect play through the corridor and punish defenders who overcommit to covering the outside overlap.

title: Front-and-Square Movement Reaction
objective: Teach players to move into a front-and-square position where they can react to a dropped mark, spoil or unpredictable football.
groundSize: Areas approximately 20 × 15 metres.
coachingDifficulty: 3 – Intermediate organisation, rotations and several observable behaviours.
setup:
Position one kicker at the edge of the area.
Place one marking player and one controlled defender approximately 15 metres away.
Position one support player five metres in front and slightly to the side of the contest.
Mark a front-and-square movement zone.
Place a finishing target beyond the contest.
howTheDrillWorks:
The kicker delivers a high football towards the marking contest.
The support player moves towards the front-and-square zone as the football travels.
The marking pair contest under controlled pressure.
The coach varies whether the football is marked, spoiled forward, spoiled sideways or deliberately brought to ground.
The support player reacts to the outcome.
If the football spills, the support player collects and accelerates into space.
If the mark is completed, the support player moves immediately into a receiving position.
The possession is transferred to the finishing target.
Players rotate through each role.
coachingPoints: Move while the football is in flight.
Position slightly in front of the contest rather than directly underneath it.
Keep enough distance to react to the spill.
Maintain vision on both the football and surrounding players.
Stay balanced and ready to move in either direction.
Accelerate through the collection.
Transition immediately into support if the mark is taken.
Communicate with the marking player.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether the support player moves before the contest occurs.
Whether the starting position allows reaction to multiple outcomes.
Whether the player avoids being drawn underneath the football.
Whether the player reacts quickly to a spill.
Whether support continues when the mark is completed.
progressions: Add an opposing front-and-square player.
Permit full legal marking pressure.
Add a second support option.
Require a kick after the ground-ball collection.
Begin from different field positions.
regressions: Use a handball feed instead of a kick.
successIndicators: Move into position before the contest.
React correctly to marks and spills.
Continue the possession after the contest.
matchApplication: Front-and-square positioning gives teams first access to footballs that spill from marking contests and provides immediate support when a teammate completes the mark.

title: Corridor-to-Width Escape Pattern
primarySkill: Changing running lanes to escape pressure
objective: Develop coordinated movement that allows a central ball carrier to escape pressure by releasing to a teammate moving into width.
groundSize: Areas approximately 25 × 18 metres.
coachingDifficulty: 4 – Advanced tactical coaching, live constraints and active correction.
setup:
Mark one central running lane and two wide escape lanes.
Position Player A with a football in the central lane.
Place one pressure defender ahead of Player A.
Position Players B and C behind and to either side.
Place a target beyond the wide gates.
howTheDrillWorks:
Player A begins carrying through the central lane.
The defender advances and closes one side of Player A’s path.
Players B and C move forward in supporting positions.
The support player on the open side accelerates towards the corresponding wide gate.
Player A scans, draws the defender and releases a handball to the open support player.
The receiver changes lane through the wide gate.
The receiver accelerates and disposes to the forward target.
The unused support player moves inside to provide the next option.
Rotate the roles after each repetition.
coachingPoints: Keep both support options alive until the defender commits.
Maintain width behind and outside the ball carrier.
Accelerate only when the open side becomes clear.
The ball carrier should engage pressure without running directly into the defender.
Handball into the receiver’s path.
The receiver must turn width into forward movement.
The unused support player should rebalance inside.
Communicate the open side early.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether the support players maintain useful width.
Whether Player A scans both sides.
Whether the defender is drawn before release.
Whether the correct wide option is selected.
Whether the receiver accelerates forward after escaping.
progressions: Add a second defender.
Allow the defender to change sides after initially committing.
Remove the marked lanes.
Continue into a second phase with another defender.
Require a kick to a leading target after the escape.
successIndicators: Recognise which side pressure has closed.
Release the football into forward space.
Reorganise support after the first disposal.
matchApplication: Teams often begin possession in the corridor but must move to width when central pressure closes. Coordinated support allows the football to escape without losing forward momentum or structure.

title: Dynamic Movement and Support Assessment
objective: Assess players’ ability to combine leading, receiving, reorientation and support movement within a continuous football sequence.
groundSize: An area approximately 40 × 25 metres divided into four connected zones.
coachingDifficulty: 4 – Advanced tactical coaching, live constraints and active correction.
setup:
Create four connected movement zones:
Lead Zone: One player completes a curved, V-cut or double-movement lead.
Reorientation Zone: The receiver turns towards one of two nominated targets.
Support Zone: A teammate provides either an overlap or underlap.
Decision Zone: The final ball carrier selects a central or wide finishing gate.
Position one controlled defender in the lead zone.
Position another controlled defender in the decision zone.
Divide players between starting and support roles.
Assign coaches to observe movement timing, balance, scanning and disposal execution.
Use Developing, Competent and Advanced ratings.
howTheDrillWorks:
The first player begins a lead in the opening zone.
A feeder delivers the football once separation is created.
The receiver marks or collects and immediately scans the next zone.
The receiver reorients towards the nominated target.
A support player provides an overlap or underlap according to the available lane.
The football is released into the support player’s running path.
The support player carries into the decision zone.
The final defender closes either the central or wide gate.
The ball carrier selects the available exit and disposes to the finishing target.
Players follow their disposal and rotate through each role.
Each player completes at least two assessed repetitions in both left- and right-side patterns.
Coaches record technical quality and decision effectiveness.
coachingPoints: Time the initial lead to the feeder.
Create genuine separation before demanding the football.
Scan before receiving whenever possible.
Reorient towards attack without becoming stationary.
Choose overlap or underlap according to the available space.
Lead moving players with the disposal.
Maintain width and safe spacing between runners.
Use the simplest available movement in the decision zone.
Continue supporting after every disposal.
Assess quality and timing rather than speed alone.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Timing and quality of the initial lead.
Balance during deceleration and directional changes.
Whether players receive while moving.
Speed and efficiency of reorientation.
Selection and timing of overlap or underlap support.
Accuracy of disposals to moving targets.
Scanning before entering the final zone.
Decision quality against the closing defender.
Continued movement after disposal.
progressions: Increase defensive pressure.
Remove nominated movement patterns.
Add a turnover transition when defenders win possession.
Introduce a scoring time limit.
Require a kick inside 50 as the final disposal.
Compare assessment results across multiple training blocks.
regressions: Predetermine the lead and support pattern.
Allow players to reset between zones.
successIndicators: Select an overlap or underlap based on space.
Recognise and attack the open finishing gate.
matchApplication: The drill replicates a complete possession sequence in which a player creates separation, receives, turns into attack and connects with teammates moving in support. It assesses whether movement skills transfer into coordinated Australian football ball movement.

title: Backpedal-to-Sprint Transition
objective: Develop the ability to move backwards under control, recognise a forward cue and transition rapidly into an effective acceleration line.
groundSize: Movement lanes approximately 15 metres long and 5 metres wide.
coachingDifficulty: 3 – Intermediate organisation, rotations and several observable behaviours.
setup:
Mark a starting line, a five-metre backpedal zone and two diagonal acceleration gates.
Position one player at the starting line facing the coach.
Place a football feeder beyond each acceleration gate.
Other players wait outside the movement lane.
Ensure the backpedal area is level and clear.
howTheDrillWorks:
The player begins in an athletic stance facing the coach.
On the first signal, the player backpedals through the marked zone using short, controlled steps.
The coach displays a left or right directional cue.
The player plants, opens the hips and turns towards the nominated gate.
The player accelerates forward through the gate.
The feeder handballs the football into the player’s running path.
The player receives, returns the handball and exits the lane.
Players rotate after every repetition.
Complete three to five turns through each gate.
coachingPoints: Keep the hips low and chest controlled while backpedalling.
Use short steps rather than reaching backwards.
Keep the feet underneath the body.
Avoid allowing the heels to become the main contact point.
Open the hips before beginning forward acceleration.
Turn through the shortest efficient path.
Locate the football immediately after turning.
Accelerate through the gate rather than slowing to receive.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether the player remains balanced while moving backwards.
Whether the feet cross during the backpedal.
Whether the hips open efficiently after the cue.
Whether acceleration begins immediately after turning.
Whether the football is received without a major reduction in speed.
progressions: Add a second directional cue during the acceleration.
Begin with lateral movement before backpedalling.
Add a chasing player.
Require a kick after receiving.
Use a bouncing football rather than a handball feed.
successIndicators: React correctly to the directional cue.
matchApplication: Players frequently move backwards while defending space, tracking a forward or reading a high football before needing to turn and sprint towards an opponent, loose football or support position.

title: Arc Run and Forward-Facing Receive
primarySkill: Arcing into a forward-facing receiving position
